content: Weet-Bix is a high-fiber breakfast cereal biscuit produced in Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa by the Sanitarium Health Food Company. The name likely derives from wheat bricks or wheat biscuits, and the plural form of Weet-Bix is generally the same as the singular. Sanitarium's wheat biscuits originated from a product called Granose, which was developed as early as the 1900s. In the 1920s, a company named Grain Products created a new sweetened biscuit called Weet-Bix. By 1930, Sanitarium acquired Grain Products, which, like Sanitarium, had ties to the Seventh-day Adventist Church. This acquisition made Weet-Bix a Sanitarium product. In Australia, Weet-Bix is considered an iconic food item and was marketed with the tagline Aussie Kids are Weet-Bix kids. In New Zealand, the slogan was adapted to Kiwi Kids are Weet-Bix kids. A similar product, Weetabix, is manufactured in England by Weetabix Limited in Kettering, Northamptonshire. The two products are nearly identical, with the main differences being that Weetabix is smaller, sweeter, and more brick-like in appearance compared to Weet-Bix. In South Africa, Weet-Bix is produced by Bokomo in Malmesbury. Weet-Bix was invented by Bennison Osborne in New South Wales, Australia, in the mid-1920s. Osborne aimed to create a more palatable product than Granose. He tested his new creation on his young nieces and nephews until he perfected it. In 1928, he registered the trademark Weetbix and began production at 659 Parramatta Road, Leichhardt, NSW, with financial backing from Arthur Shannon. Osborne's marketing partner, Macfarlane (Mac), proved to be an excellent marketer. The product's success was so rapid that by October 1928, it became evident that the Australian market alone could not meet the demand. With Shannon's financial support, factories were established in Auckland and Christchurch, New Zealand. The enterprise was so successful that Shannon sold his stake in 1930 to the Sanitarium Health Food Company. Osborne and Mac then exported the product to South Africa, where they secured additional financial backing and set up a factory in Cape Town, forming the British & African Cereal Company Pty. This company was registered in London, with Osborne serving as Managing Director. To differentiate the product in England, it was decided to market it under the name Weetabix. In England, Osborne and Mac became joint Managing Directors, with Osborne overseeing production and Mac handling marketing. After evaluating 33 potential factory sites, Burton Latimer was chosen, partly due to the availability of a disused flour mill offered by a Mr. George, who was given shares in the company. When the business was firmly established, Shannon offered to finance its expansion, but the company's cash flow was strong enough that additional funding was unnecessary. Shannon did, however, suggest exploring the Canadian market. At this point, Mac left the business to pursue overseas ventures, leaving Osborne as the sole Managing Director, with Mr. George serving as Chairman of Directors. A fleet of cars was purchased, and salesmen were employed across England. Osborne eventually became the wartime supervisor of the Army Air Force Base in Zephyr Hills, Florida. After the war, in 1946, he returned to Australia with his wife and three daughters, where he passed away in 1980. Weet-Bix competes closely with Nutri-Grain, produced by the market-dominant Kellogg's company, for the title of Australia's best-selling cereal. The two brands have clashed in television advertising. Kellogg's aired an ad mocking the supposedly bland taste of Weet-Bix, to which Sanitarium responded with a commercial highlighting the high sugar content of Nutri-Grain. This campaign negatively impacted Nutri-Grain's sales. It was rumored that the two companies later agreed to a truce, refraining from disparaging each other's products in future advertising. In Australia, as of March 2006, the Weet-Bix jingle included the line, Hope you've had your Weet-Bix, all-Australian Weet-Bix, for breakfast every day. The phrase I hope he's had his Weet-Bix today or similar variations is commonly used in Australian sports commentary. For example, SBS commentator Simon Hill remarked, Cahill is ecstatic. He did have his Weet-Bix this morning, after Tim Cahill scored Australia's first goal at the 2006 World Cup against Japan. The Weet-Bix trademark has been recognized as Australia's favorite trademark by IP Australia, a federal government department.
